items.title: Analytic topology and finite smooth algebraic stratifications of complex varieties
items.statement:
Let $X$ be a classical algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of [[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]: a separated quasi-compact locally ringed space over $\mathbb C$ with a finite cover by affine models $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the morphisms being the regular maps, i.e. the morphisms of locally ringed spaces over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]]).

(a) **Analytic topology.** An affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ carries the subspace topology of the Euclidean topology of $\mathbb C^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). If $Z_1,Z_2\subseteq X$ are affine models and $\varphi:Z_1\to Z_2$ is the structure-sheaf isomorphism, then on $Z_1\cap Z_2$ the maps $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are given locally by polynomial quotient functions and are therefore continuous for the Euclidean topologies. Hence the topologies transported from the two affine models agree on the overlap, so the affine-model topologies glue to a unique topology on the underlying set of $X$ ([[def-topological-space]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]): the **analytic topology** of $X$. Every regular map of complex classical varieties is continuous for the analytic topologies, and the analytic topology refines the Zariski topology because polynomial zero sets are Euclidean closed. Whenever a complex algebraic variety is used as a topological space below it carries the analytic topology, and each subvariety carries the subspace topology.

(b) **Smooth points.** Let $S$ be a classical variety over $\mathbb C$ and $x\in S$. The point $x$ is a **smooth point of $S$** if its algebraic local ring $\mathcal O_{S,x}$ is a regular local ring: a nonzero Noetherian local ring whose maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_x$ satisfies $\dim_{\mathbb C}(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2)=\dim\mathcal O_{S,x}$ ([[def-embedding-dimension-and-regular-local-ring]]). The residue field at a classical complex point is $\mathbb C$. The variety $S$ is **smooth** if every point is smooth. This intrinsic algebraic condition does not require a Zariski neighbourhood to be algebraically isomorphic to an open subset of affine space.

(c) **Finite smooth algebraic stratifications.** A **finite smooth algebraic stratification with the frontier condition** of $X$ is a finite decomposition $X=\coprod_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha$ into pairwise disjoint nonempty connected locally closed subsets $S_\alpha\subseteq X$ - the **strata** - such that each $S_\alpha$, with its reduced induced algebraic structure (locally the polynomial-quotient function sheaf on the locally closed algebraic set), is a smooth algebraic subvariety of $X$, and such that for every $\alpha$ the closure $\overline{S_\alpha}$ of $S_\alpha$ in $X$ is a union of strata. The latter is the **frontier condition**: the frontier $\overline{S_\alpha}\setminus S_\alpha$ of every stratum is a union of strata. An open subset of an affine model is a union of principal open subsets, and each principal open subset is again an affine model, so every locally closed subvariety of $X$ is a classical variety for the induced structure sheaf.
items.strategy: Every clause is a definition together with its well-definedness check; no existence theorem for stratifications is asserted. (i) Analytic topology: on the intersection of two affine models the transition isomorphism and its inverse are regular, so locally they are polynomial quotient functions, which are Euclidean-continuous; a topology transported along such a homeomorphism is equal to the restriction of the transported topology on the overlap, and the glued topology on $X$ is therefore forced and unique. Continuity of regular maps and the comparison with the Zariski topology (whose open sets are complements of Euclidean-closed polynomial zero sets) are checked in the same local coordinates. (ii) Smoothness is the intrinsic regular-local-ring condition of [[def-embedding-dimension-and-regular-local-ring]] on the algebraic stalk. An isomorphism of classical varieties induces an isomorphism of its local ring, maximal ideal and cotangent space, so the condition is chart-independent. This definition asserts no existence of smooth strata and no analytic-chart comparison theorem. (iii) A locally closed subvariety has its own reduced polynomial-quotient function sheaf; the inverse-image of the ambient structure sheaf is not substituted for that quotient structure. (iii) Strata: a locally closed $S\subseteq X$ is open in its closure, so intersecting the finite affine cover of $X$ with $S$ and using that principal open subsets $D(h)$ of an affine model are affine models exhibits $S$ as a classical variety with the induced structure sheaf. (iv) The frontier condition is a condition on the given finite partition only. No choice principle is used: nothing is selected, and all cited suppliers are choice-free.
items.axiom_use: None: the definition is choice-free and makes no selection; the cited published suppliers are stated without choice.

items.title: Locally constant sheaves of finite rank
items.statement:
Let $S$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), let $k$ be a field and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of $k$-vector spaces on $S$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[def-presheaf-of-groups-rings-modules]]). Then $\mathcal F$ is **locally constant of finite rank** if every point $x\in S$ has an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq S$ for which there are an integer $n\ge0$ and an isomorphism of sheaves on $U$
$$\mathcal F|_U\;\cong\;k_U^{\,n},$$
where $k_U$ is the constant sheaf on $U$ with value $k$ and $\mathcal F|_U$ is the restriction of $\mathcal F$ to the open subspace $U$ ([[def-restriction-sheaf-open-subspace]], [[def-morphism-of-presheaves]], [[lem-constant-sheaf-is-the-sheaf-of-locally-constant-functions]]). A sheaf with this property is also called a **finite-rank local system of $k$-vector spaces** on $S$. This is a property of the sheaf on the space; no identification of such sheaves with functors on the fundamental groupoid is part of the definition.
items.strategy: The definition is read literally: near each point there is an isomorphism onto a finite free constant sheaf. The constant sheaf $k_U^n$ is the $n$-fold direct sum of $k_U$, whose sections are the locally constant $k$-valued functions ([[lem-constant-sheaf-is-the-sheaf-of-locally-constant-functions]]); restricting a sheaf to an open subspace is the construction of [[def-restriction-sheaf-open-subspace]]; an isomorphism of sheaves is a morphism of presheaves ([[def-morphism-of-presheaves]]) with a two-sided inverse. The integer $n$ is quantified locally, so no global rank is asserted, and the final sentence only records that a functorial groupoid presentation is a different, uncompared object.

items.title: Algebraically constructible complexes of analytic field sheaves
items.statement:
Let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety, i.e. a classical algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), regarded as a topological space with its analytic topology ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]), and let $k$ be a field. Write $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ for the category of sheaves of $k$-vector spaces and $k$-linear morphisms ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[def-presheaf-of-groups-rings-modules]], [[def-module-on-ringed-space]]); it is an abelian category ([[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]]), so its bounded derived category $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is defined with the conventions of [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]], under the standing smallness hypothesis recorded there.

The category $D_c^b(X;k)$ is the full subcategory of $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ consisting of the complexes $A$ satisfying:

1. $A$ is **cohomologically bounded**: $H^j(A)=0$ for $|j|$ sufficiently large; and
2. $A$ is **algebraically constructible**: there exists a finite smooth algebraic stratification with the frontier condition $\mathfrak S$ of $X$ ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]) such that for every stratum $S\in\mathfrak S$ and every integer $j$ the restriction $H^j(A)|_S$ is locally constant of finite rank ([[def-locally-constant-sheaf-of-finite-rank]]).

These are topological constructible sheaves, not coherent or quasi-coherent sheaves. We use the shift convention of [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]: $H^j(A[m])=H^{j+m}(A)$. A groupoid local system is identified with a locally constant sheaf only through an explicit local comparison, which is not made here.
items.strategy: Every clause is definitional. The analytic topology and the stratification convention come from [[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]], local constancy from [[def-locally-constant-sheaf-of-finite-rank]], and the derived category with its shift convention from [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]; abelianness of $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ is the published abelian-category theorem for modules over the ringed space $(X,k_X)$ ([[def-module-on-ringed-space]]). Cohomological boundedness and constructibility are conditions on the cohomology sheaves of a bounded complex; shifting replaces $H^j$ by $H^{j+m}$, which preserves a bounded range, so the class is shift-stable by construction. Constructibility quantifies existentially over finite smooth algebraic frontier stratifications: no stratification is fixed, and no existence or common-refinement theorem for stratifications is asserted. No choice principle is used.

items.title: Analytic field sheaves have injective derived models
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a topological space and let $k$ be a field. The category $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ of sheaves of $k$-vector spaces is the category of modules over the ringed space $(X,k_X)$ with constant structure sheaf $k_X$ ([[def-locally-ringed-space]], [[def-module-on-ringed-space]]); it is a locally small Grothendieck category and carries a functorial injective embedding, and iterating that embedding on cokernels yields for every $k$-sheaf one specific injective resolution ([[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]). These resolutions are bounded-below injective replacements, so with the dependent choice supplied by AC ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]) the bounded-below injective complexes model the bounded derived category: $K^+(\operatorname{Inj}\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))\to D^+(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is an equivalence, and morphisms of the bounded derived category are computed by these replacements ([[thm-injective-complexes-model-the-bounded-below-derived-category]]).

Now let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety and let $\mathfrak S$ be a finite smooth algebraic stratification with the frontier condition of $X$ ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). Let $D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ be the full subcategory of $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ of complexes whose cohomology sheaves are bounded and constructible with respect to $\mathfrak S$ ([[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]]). Then $D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ is a triangulated subcategory: it is closed under shifts, isomorphisms and mapping cones. More generally, if two bounded algebraically constructible complexes are constructible with respect to one common finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification, then their cone is bounded and constructible with respect to that stratification.
items.strategy: Identify Sh_k(X) with Mod(k_X); the published module-sheaf lemma supplies local smallness, Grothendieck structure and functorial injective embeddings. With AC⇒DC, lem-bounded-below-complexes-admit-injective-replacements supplies replacements of complexes, and the bounded-below model theorem computes bounded derived morphisms. Step 1.2 splits local-system extensions by finite quotient-basis germ lifts and gluing locally constant scalar multiples, with an explicit inverse and no connected-neighborhood hypothesis. Exact inverse image preserves bounded roofs and cones; finite matrix-coordinate constancy gives finite-rank kernels and cokernels on each stratum. The cone long exact sequence and local extension splitting give constructibility and finite cohomological support. Zero objects, finite sums, shifts and cones show the full subcategory is triangulated for one common supplied stratification.
items.axiom_use: AC is used exactly through the functorial injective-embedding theorem for the Grothendieck category $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ (which produces the functorial injective resolutions) and through AC $\Rightarrow$ DC for the bounded-below injective model equivalence. The constructibility closure argument is choice-free. No other choice principle is used.

items.title: Finite poset diagrams have bounded finite bar models
items.statement: Let $P$ be a finite nonempty poset, regarded as a category with one arrow $p\to q$ exactly when $p\le q$, and let $h$ be the largest number of strict inequalities in a chain of $P$. Let $\operatorname{Diag}_k(P)$ be the abelian category of covariant diagrams of $k$-vector spaces on $P$, i.e. the functor category of $k$-vector spaces indexed by $P$, with its cochain complexes as in [[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]]. If $M$ is a bounded complex of diagrams in $\operatorname{Diag}_k(P)$ whose vector spaces are finite-dimensional and vanish outside internal degrees $[a,b]$, then the derived inverse limit $\mathbf R\lim M:=\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}(\underline k,M)$ ([[def-derived-hom-in-the-bounded-setting]]) has a finite-dimensional cochain model concentrated in $[a,b+h]$. If $A,B$ are such complexes, concentrated in $[a,b]$ and $[c,d]$ respectively, then their derived Hom has a finite-dimensional cochain model concentrated in $[c-b,d-a+h]$. These models commute with every field extension. For the empty poset, the diagram sections and the derived Hom model are zero by convention.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Kernels, images and cokernels of morphisms of diagrams of $k$-vector spaces are formed objectwise, so a morphism of diagrams is an epimorphism exactly when it is surjective at every object, and a complex of diagrams is exact exactly when it is exact at every object. In particular exactness questions about $\operatorname{Diag}_k(P)$ reduce to the vector spaces $N(p)$, and no diagram-level machinery beyond the objectwise one is used below. [given, algebra]

2.1 For $p\in P$ define the diagram $Q_p$ by $Q_p(q)=k$ for $p\le q$ and $Q_p(q)=0$ otherwise, with the identity as structure map whenever both values are nonzero. A natural transformation $\varphi:Q_p\to N$ is determined by $\varphi_p(1)\in N(p)$, since for $q\ge p$ the component $\varphi_q$ must equal $N(p\to q)\circ\varphi_p$ and for $q\ngeq p$ the source $Q_p(q)$ is zero; conversely every vector $v\in N(p)$ extends by these formulas. Hence $\operatorname{Hom}(Q_p,N)\cong N(p)$ by evaluation at $p$. Pulling back along the identification, a surjection $\pi:N\to N'$ induces the surjection $N(p)\to N'(p)$ by step 1.1, so every map $Q_p\to N'$ lifts to $N$ and $Q_p$ is projective. For a finite-dimensional $V$, a natural transformation $Q_p\otimes_kV\to N$ is likewise determined by its value at $p$, a $k$-linear map $V\to N(p)$, and conversely every such map extends uniquely by the structure maps of $N$, so $\operatorname{Hom}(Q_p\otimes_kV,N)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_k(V,N(p))$; since $\operatorname{Hom}_k(V,-)$ carries surjections to surjections — lift the images of a finite basis and extend linearly — the diagram $Q_p\otimes_kV$ is projective as well. A finite direct sum of projectives is projective, because $\operatorname{Hom}(\bigoplus_tX_t,N)\cong\prod_t\operatorname{Hom}(X_t,N)$ and a finite product of surjections of vector spaces is surjective by induction on the number of factors. Only finitely many basis vectors and summands occur at each step, so no choice principle is used. [step 1.1, algebra, construct]

3.1 For a diagram $N$ put $\mathcal B_n(N)=\bigoplus_{p_0<\cdots<p_n}Q_{p_n}\otimes_kN(p_0)$ for $n\ge0$, with the face maps $\partial_i:\mathcal B_n(N)\to\mathcal B_{n-1}(N)$ ($n\ge1$, $0\le i\le n$) given on the summand of the chain $p_0<\cdots<p_n$ by: for $i=0$ apply the structure map $N(p_0)\to N(p_1)$ and delete $p_0$; for $0<i<n$ delete the inner vertex $p_i$, keeping the coefficient in $N(p_0)$ and the representable index $p_n$; for $i=n$ delete $p_n$ and use the natural map $Q_{p_n}\to Q_{p_{n-1}}$ (the identity where the source is $k$, and zero otherwise) while keeping the coefficient. Let $\partial=\sum_i(-1)^i\partial_i$ for $n\ge1$ and set $\partial=0$ in bar degree zero, before adjoining the augmentation. The simplicial identities $\partial_i\partial_j=\partial_{j-1}\partial_i$ for $i<j$ hold because diagram transport $p\mapsto N(p)$ is functorial and the maps between representables compose, so $\partial^2=0$; this is a sign-alternating sum of a simplicial identity. Since chains of $P$ have at most $h$ strict inequalities, $\mathcal B_n(N)=0$ for $n>h$. Augment by the structure maps $\epsilon:\mathcal B_0(N)\to N$, $Q_p\otimes_kN(p)\to N$, which are natural. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Evaluate the augmented complex at $q\in P$. Its degree-$n$ part consists of the chains $p_0<\cdots<p_n\le q$ with a vector of $N(p_0)$, the faces delete a vertex as in step 3.1, the last face being free to delete $q$, and the augmentation sends a length-zero chain $(p_0)$ to $N(p_0\to q)v$. Define a degree-$(-1)$-to-$0$ map $s_{-1}:N(q)\to\mathcal B_0(N)(q)$ by $v\mapsto(q,v)$, and for $n\ge0$ a degree-$n$-to-$n+1$ map $s_n$ on the summand of the chain $p_0<\cdots<p_n\le q$ by $s_n(v)=(-1)^{n+1}(p_0<\cdots<p_n<q,\,v)$ when $p_n<q$, and $s_n=0$ when $p_n=q$. One checks $\partial s_n+s_{n-1}\partial=\mathrm{id}$ on each evaluated component: the appended simplex contributes through its last face with sign $(-1)^{n+1}\cdot(-1)^{n+1}=1$, every other face is matched by the corresponding appended term in $s\partial$ with opposite sign, and in degree zero the augmentation section cancels exactly the last-face term; when $p_n=q$ and $n\ge1$, only the last face contributes to $s_{n-1}\partial$, with coefficient $(-1)^n(-1)^n=1$, while for $n=0$ the term $s_{-1}\epsilon$ is the identity. Moreover $\epsilon$ is surjective on the evaluated complexes because $(q,v)\mapsto v$, so the augmented evaluated complex is exact in every degree. Exactness is objectwise by step 1.1, so $\epsilon:\mathcal B(N)\to N$ is a quasi-isomorphism; and if every $N(p)$ is finite-dimensional then every $\mathcal B_n(N)$ is a finite direct sum of projectives by step 2.1, so $\mathcal B(N)$ is a bounded projective resolution of $N$. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Let $A$ be a bounded complex of diagrams with finite-dimensional values, vanishing outside internal degrees $[a,b]$, with internal differentials $d_A$. Apply the bar construction of step 4.1 to each internal degree $u$, so $\mathcal B_n(A^u)$ has bar degree $n\in[0,h]$ and carries the internal differential $d_A:\mathcal B_n(A^u)\to\mathcal B_n(A^{u+1})$. The face maps $\partial$ commute with the maps induced by $d_A$, since they are built from the structure maps of the diagrams and from the fixed maps between representables. Take the total complex $\operatorname{Tot}$ with $\operatorname{Tot}^m=\bigoplus_{u-n=m}\mathcal B_n(A^u)$ and differential $D=d_A+(-1)^u\partial$ on the summand $\mathcal B_n(A^u)$; the sign $(-1)^u$ makes the horizontal and vertical parts anticommute, so $D^2=0$. Each column $u$ maps quasi-isomorphically to $A^u$ by step 4.1, so the rows of the mapping cone of $\operatorname{Tot}\to A$ are the mapping cones of the augmentations $\mathcal B(A^u)\to A^u$ and are acyclic; a bounded double complex with acyclic rows has acyclic total complex, by filtering by the finitely many internal degrees and inducting on the number of rows with the long exact homology sequence of the quotient by the top row. Hence $\operatorname{Tot}\to A$ is a quasi-isomorphism, $\operatorname{Tot}$ is a complex of finite-dimensional projective diagrams by steps 2.1 and 4.1, and its total degrees $u-n$ lie in $[a-h,b]$. [F2, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

5.2 Resolve the constant diagram $\underline k$ by its bar complex $\mathcal B(\underline k)$, a bounded complex of finite-dimensional projective diagrams of the form of step 4.1 with $\underline k$ in internal degree $0$. These bounded projective models require no DC: Hom from a single projective into an acyclic complex is acyclic by exactness of its Hom functor; filtering a bounded projective complex by its finitely many degrees and applying the cohomology sequence to the resulting termwise split Hom sequences proves the same for that complex. Hence Hom from the model preserves quasi-isomorphisms and computes [F1] without any infinite sequence of lifts. Then $\mathbf R\lim M=\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}(\underline k,M)$ is computed by the Hom complex $Q\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\mathcal B(\underline k),M)$ of [F1], whose degree-$r$ term is $\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal B(\underline k)^i,M^{i+r})$. Here $\mathcal B(\underline k)^{-n}=\bigoplus_{p_0<\cdots<p_n}Q_{p_n}$ is nonzero only for $0\le n\le h$ and $M^j=0$ for $j\notin[a,b]$, so by the vanishing rule of [F1] nonzero factors require $a-r\le i\le b$ with $-h\le i\le0$, so any nonzero factor has $r\in[a,b+h]$. Concretely the bar-degree-$n$ part is the finite product $\prod_{p_0<\cdots<p_n}M(p_n)$, so every term is a finite product of finite-dimensional spaces, hence finite-dimensional. Thus $\mathbf R\lim M$ has a finite-dimensional cochain model concentrated in $[a,b+h]$. [F1, F3, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 For the pair $A,B$ concentrated in $[a,b]$ and $[c,d]$, resolve the source by the total bar model $P_A:=\operatorname{Tot}$ of step 5.1, concentrated in $[a-h,b]$, and apply [F1]: $\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}(A,B)$ is computed by $Q\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(P_A,B)$, whose degree-$r$ term is the finite product $\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}(P_A^i,B^{i+r})$. A nonzero factor requires $P_A^i\ne0$ and $B^{i+r}\ne0$, hence $a-h\le i\le b$ and $c\le i+r\le d$; so for $r<c-b$ every $i$ with $P_A^i\ne0$ has $i+r\le b+r<c$ and for $r>d-a+h$ every such $i$ has $i+r>d$, and in both cases every factor of the term vanishes. Thus the model is concentrated in $[c-b,d-a+h]$. By the evaluation identity in step 2.1, each summand with $u-n=i$ and chain $p_0<\cdots<p_n$ contributes $\operatorname{Hom}_k(A^u(p_0),B^{i+r}(p_n))$. Thus every term is a finite product of Hom spaces between finite-dimensional vector spaces, hence finite-dimensional. [F1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Let $K/k$ be a field extension, and write the base-changed inputs as $K\otimes_kM$, $K\otimes_kA$, $K\otimes_kB$, diagrams over $K$. The models built in steps 5.2 and 6.1 have terms obtained from the values $M(p)$, $\operatorname{Hom}_k(A(p),B(q))$ by finite sums, finite products and the fixed face and structure maps; extending scalars commutes with finite direct sums, with finite products and, between finite-dimensional spaces, with Hom spaces, so $K\otimes_k$ of the model for $(M,A,B)$ is the model for the base-changed inputs, with the same signs and differentials. Tensoring with $K$ preserves kernels and images of linear maps between finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces and hence commutes with the homology of a bounded complex of such spaces, so the cohomology of the base-changed model is the base change of the cohomology of the original model. This proves both base-change assertions. For the empty poset there are no chains, the diagram sections and the Hom complex vanish by the same product formulas, and the asserted model is zero. [step 5.2, step 6.1, algebra] ∎
items.axiom_use: None: all constructions are finite direct sums, finite products and Hom spaces of finite-dimensional vector spaces.

items.title: Locally contractible metric spaces have singular constant sheaf cohomology
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) having a neighbourhood basis of contractible open sets at every point, and let $k$ be a field. Write $k_X$ for its constant sheaf. There are natural isomorphisms
$$H^q(X,k_X)\cong H^q_{\operatorname{sing}}(X;k)$$
in every degree, where the left side is derived cohomology in the category of sheaves of $k$-vector spaces (computed with the functorial $k$-linear injective resolutions supplied by [[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]; compare [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). The same assertion holds on every open subset of $X$. In particular a nonempty contractible space with this local property has constant-sheaf cohomology $k$ in degree zero and zero otherwise. This applies to every finite-polyhedral open star and to its nonempty intersection with a closed simplex.
items.strategy: Steps 1.1–2.1 prove flasque acyclicity in k-linear and abelian sheaves and construct global singular-cochain representatives using a locally finite shrinking on the open metric subspace U, with closure containment in representative domains. Step 3.1 uses filtered-colimit exactness, the actual alternating point cochain differential, and the acyclic-resolution theorem with injective data on all successive kernels. Step 3.2 identifies the canonical sheafification kernel as the directed union of acyclic duals of small-chain quotients; AC supplies the degreewise vector-space complements. Step 4.1 obtains naturality from the canonical cochain pullback and augmentation. Step 5.1 gives explicit carrier-simplex contractions of N_delta neighborhoods, stars and star/closed-simplex intersections. No ambient convexity or derived face-diagram equivalence is asserted.
items.axiom_use: AC supplies metric paracompactness and cover shrinking; k-linear and abelian functorial injective data; DC for delta functors and acyclic-resolution comparison; flasque section lifting; local cochain representatives, refinement indices and simplex assignments; and degreewise complements for possibly infinite-dimensional acyclic chain complexes. Finite-polyhedral contractions are explicit and choice-free.

items.title: Point operations and the open closed constructible line
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and let $k$ be a field. (1) The constructible category of a point is the bounded derived category of finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces, $D_c^b(\operatorname{pt};k)\simeq D^b(k\text{-}\mathbf{Vect}^{\mathrm{fd}})$ ([[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]]). For the identity map of the point, all four pullback/pushforward operations $f^*,f_*,f_!,f^!$ are the identity functors of that category, the tensor product and internal Hom are the usual finite cochain constructions, and the dualizing object is $k$ concentrated in degree $0$ ([[lem-bounded-analytic-field-sheaves-have-derived-tensor-hom-and-pullback-pushforward-adjunctions]], [[def-derived-operations-on-analytic-sheaves-over-locally-compact-spaces]]). (2) On the complex line with the open inclusion $j:\mathbb C^*\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$ and the closed inclusion $i:\{0\}\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$, there is a $k$-linear short exact sequence of sheaves
$$0\to j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}\to k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k\to0,$$
and its associated exact triangle is the ordinary localization triangle of the constructible derived category.
items.strategy: (1) A sheaf on the point is its vector space of sections, so a bounded complex of $k$-sheaves on the point is a bounded complex of $k$-vector spaces, and the single-stratum stratification of the point makes constructibility exactly the condition of finite-dimensional cohomology; a bounded complex with finite-dimensional cohomology is isomorphic in the derived category to a bounded complex of finite-dimensional vector spaces (truncate outside the cohomological support and split the resulting finite complex), so $D_c^b(\operatorname{pt};k)\simeq D^b(k\text{-}\mathbf{Vect}^{\mathrm{fd}})$ via the injective derived model of [[lem-field-module-sheaves-have-injective-derived-models]]. The identity map is proper with exact inverse and direct images, so $f^*=f_*=\operatorname{id}$ and $f_!=f_*=\operatorname{id}$ on these categories, and dually $f^!$, being right adjoint to $f_!$, is also the identity; tensor and internal Hom are the signed total tensor and Hom complex of finite-dimensional complexes, and the dualizing object of the $0$-dimensional smooth point is $k$ in degree $0$ ([[lem-bounded-analytic-field-sheaves-have-derived-tensor-hom-and-pullback-pushforward-adjunctions]], [[def-derived-operations-on-analytic-sheaves-over-locally-compact-spaces]]; these two interfaces are declared forward references, closed later in this run). (2) Specialize the published open/closed sequence to the constant sheaf $\mathcal F=k_{\mathbb C}$ ([[lem-extension-by-zero-short-exact-sequence]]): it reads $0\to j_!(k_{\mathbb C^*})\to k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*(k)\to0$, with $j_!$ the extension by zero of [[thm-extension-by-zero-adjunction-exactness]] and with the sheaf supported at $0$ identified as a pushforward by [[lem-sheaf-supported-on-a-closed-subset-is-a-pushforward]]; exactness is the published stalk computation. The mapping cone of $k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k$ is quasi-isomorphic to $j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}[1]$ ([[def-mapping-cone-of-a-chain-map]]), so rotating the cone triangle gives $j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}\to k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k\to j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}[1]$, the localization triangle of the derived category ([[thm-the-derived-category-inherits-a-triangulated-structure]]).
